case_name: Islamic Schools Federation of Ontario v. Ottawa Board of Education
text:
Ontario Court (General Division), Divisional Court

Citation: Islamic Schools Federation of Ontario v. Ottawa
Board of Education

Court File: 1082/96

Date: 1997-04-21

O'Leary, Soublière and Corbett JJ.

Counsel:

Emilio Binavince

and
Shelden P. Massie
,
for applicants.

Brian A. Crane
,
Q.C., for respondent.

Robert E. Charney
,
for intervener.

The judgment of the court was delivered by

O'LEARY J.:—

Case Summary

[
1
]

The Islamic Schools Federation of
Ontario and Abdul-Kareem Abdul-Aziz, by his litigation guardian, Sharon
Fongenie, apply in effect for judicial review of the refusal of the Ottawa
Board of Education to close its schools on two major Muslim holy days. The
applicants ask for a declaration that the Board has a duty to consider the
request of the applicants that schools be closed on those days and to close
such schools on one or both such holy days where the number of students of the
Islamic faith justify such closing.

[
2
]

In the alternative, the applicants ask
for a declaration that paragraphs 5, 7 and 8 of section 2, subsection (4) of
Regulation 304, the school year and school holidays regulation made pursuant to
the
Education Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. E.2, are invalid, being inconsistent
with their freedom of conscience and religion and their equality rights under

sections 2
(
a
) and
15
respectively of the
Canadian Charter of Rights
and Freedoms
.
The paragraphs attacked provide for school holidays at
Christmas time, on Good Friday and on Easter Monday.

[
3
]

The application is based on the
proposition that Regulation 304 recognizes and provides for school holidays on
the Christian holy days of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday and so such
holidays have a religious purpose. Thus, it is argued that to avoid infringing
the applicants' rights to freedom of religion under
s. 2
(a)
of the
Charter

and to equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination under

section 15(1)
of the
Charter
, the Board, if it is free to do so under
Regulation 304, must close certain of its schools as requested on the Muslim
holy days. If the Board is not free to close those schools as requested, then
the paragraphs of Regulation 304 already identified must be struck down.

[
4
]

Both the Supreme Court of Canada and
the Court of Appeal for Ontario have made clear that, although such days as Sundays,
Christmas and Easter were historically celebrated as holidays for religious
reasons, they have over the years become secular holidays or common pause days.
A school calendar which includes holidays for Christmas and Good Friday is to
"be taken to be secular in nature and thus neutral or non-discriminatory
on its face":
Commission scolaire régionale de Chambly v. Bergevin
,

1994 CanLII 102 (SCC)
,
[1994] 2 S.C.R. 525
at 540,
115 D.L.R. (4th) 609
. In the absence of any
evidence that the impugned school holidays were chosen for a religious purpose
rather than a secular purpose, I conclude they were chosen for a secular
purpose. Since Regulation 304 does not create holidays so that Christian holy
days can be observed and since
s. 21(2)
(
g
) of the
Education Act
provides
that a child is excused from attendance at school on any day regarded as a holy
day by the religion to which the child belongs, Regulation 304 does not
infringe Muslims' freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed by
s. 2
(a)

of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.

[
5
]

Neither does Regulation 304 directly
discriminate against Muslims so as to contravene their
s. 15

Charter
right
to equal protection and benefit of the law. Assuming that Muslims suffer
adverse effect discrimination through Muslim students having to miss two school
days each year to observe their high holy days of Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha,
while Christian students miss no time because their holy days fall on the
school holidays provided for by Regulation 304, the Regulation does not offend
s. 15 of the
Charter.
The legislature, in advancing the secular goal of
providing for school holidays that can be enjoyed by students and parents in
common with those who work in banks, government offices and most professional
retail and business establishments, could not have chosen holidays that
interfere less with the Muslims' holy days and the Muslims' right to equal
protection and benefit of the law.

[
6
]

If there be any infringement of that
right, such is demonstrably justified as being a reasonable limit on that right
in a free and democratic society. Regulation 304 does not then offend the
Charter
.

[
7
]

Again, assuming Muslims suffer adverse
effect discrimination by having to miss school on their holy days, then the
duty to accommodate, that is to say to relieve against the disadvantage
suffered by reasonable means short of hardship, has been fulfilled by the
Board, in the manner outlined in these reasons.

[
8
]

The Board then was under no obligation
to agree to the request that it make the two Muslim high holy days into school
holidays or to study the question of doing so. The application therefore must
be dismissed.

The Background

Requirements of the Education Act

[
9
]

The
Education Act
and
regulations thereunder establish the requirements for the school year in
Ontario. Under section 11, the Minister of Education and Training (hereinafter
the "Minister"), subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor
in Council, may make regulations prescribing and governing the school year,
school terms and school holidays and permitting school boards to designate, and
to implement with the prior approval of the Minister, a school year, school
terms and school holidays for schools under their jurisdiction. Pursuant to
these provisions, Regulation 304, R.R.O. 1990 entitled "School Year and School
Holidays" was passed.

Regulation 304 reads in part:

2(1) Subject to section 5, the school year shall commence on
or after the 1st day of September and end on or before the 30th day of June.

(2) Subject to section 5, a school
year shall include a minimum of 194 school days of which up to 9 days may be
designated by the board as professional activity days and the remaining school
days shall be instructional days.

* * * * *

(4) Subject to section 5, the following are school holidays:

1. Every Saturday and Sunday.

2. When the school is open during July, Canada Day.

3. Labour Day.

4. A day appointed by the Governor General or the Lieutenant
Governor as a public holiday or for Thanksgiving.

5. A Christmas vacation consisting of fourteen consecutive
days commencing on the Monday next following the Friday preceding the 21st day
of December, but when the 21st day of December is a Thursday or a Friday,
commencing on the Monday next following.

6. Five consecutive days commencing on the Monday next
following the Friday preceding the 14th day of March.

7. Good Friday.

8. Easter Monday.

9. Victoria Day.

* * * * *

5(1) For one or more schools under its jurisdiction a board
may designate a school year and school holidays that are different from those
prescribed in
section 2
and ... the board may, upon approval thereof by the
Minister, implement such school calendar.

[
10
]

As a result of the holidays provided
for by Regulation 304, there were only 197 school days available for the school
year from September 1, 1994 to June 30, 1995 and if the school year was to
commence after Labour day, there were only 195 school days available. If school
were to open the day after Labour Day, namely September 6, 1994 and close on
June 29, 1995, then the required 194 school days would have been provided for.
Such might be considered to be the traditional school year. Below is a calendar
showing the 1994-95 school year with holidays as provided for by Regulation
304.

[
11
]

The Board is required to submit to the
Minister for approval, on or before the first day of May in each year, a school
calendar to be followed by the schools under its jurisdiction for the following
school year. The following process is followed with respect to the
establishment of a system-wide school year for the elementary and secondary
schools under the jurisdiction of the Board.

[
12
]

First, the Ministry of Education and
Training (hereinafter the "Ministry") issues instructions and a five
year calendar of school days and school holidays. Second, the Board, after
extensive consultation, prepares, adopts and submits to the Minister for
approval a system-wide school calendar for all elementary and secondary
schools.

[
13
]

Because of the prescribed requirements,
a board has very little flexibility in making adjustments to the school calendar
proposed by the Ministry. Also according to the Director of Education for the
Board, as a general principle, it is desirable from an administrative and an
educational point of view for teaching to be carried out, so far as possible,
on a continuous basis without interruption for days off in the middle of a
school week.

[
14
]

For at least the past 15 years the
school calendar established by the Board has provided for nine professional
activity days. In the secondary schools, six of these professional activity days
fall at the end of the school year. These days are necessary for the purpose of
marking examinations, consultations with respect to student promotion from one
grade to another and for college or university admission, and preparation for
and the conduct of commencement ceremonies. The inclusion of nine professional
activity days in the school year is also a requirement of the collective
agreements between the Board and its teachers and has been a requirement of
collective agreements for some time.

[
15
]

Prior to 1994, apart from the
designated statutory holidays referred to in Regulation 304, the Board has
never closed its school system, or any particular school, for the observance of
a religious holiday. In fact, apart from emergencies, the Board has never closed
a school, with the exception of the prescribed holidays and the professional
activity days most of which fall, as noted above, after final examinations at
the end of the school year.

[
16
]

For the school year 1994-95, however,
the Board with the approval of the Minister, delayed the opening of the school
year until September 7 to avoid disruption that would otherwise have been
caused by the two Jewish holy days celebrating Rosh Hashanah. The circumstances
surrounding this decision I will describe later.

Observance of Holy Days

[
17
]

The
Education Act
provides:

21(2) A child is excused from attendance at school if,

* * * * *

(g)
the child is absent on a day regarded as a holy day
by the church or religious denomination to which the child belongs;

[
18
]

All schools under the jurisdiction of
the Board are instructed as to this requirement and in addition directed not to
call meetings or conduct significant events for students, staff or the
community on such holy days. Since 1985, directives have been sent out by the
Board to all schools with respect to the observance of holy days.

[
19
]

For example, on January 30, 1986, the
Director of Education sent the following memorandum to all principals in the
elementary and secondary schools:

On August 29, 1985, you received two calendars of special days
observed by members of various ethnocultural and religious backgrounds. You may
recall that specific dates for the second calendar covering January to June,
1986 were not available at that time. These dates are now available and an updated
calendar is attached.

Please note that students may need to be absent on certain
holy days as marked with an asterisk on the calendar. May I draw your attention
to these specifically. In recognition of the Jewish Passover, you are asked not
to call meetings or conduct significant events for students, staff or community
on April 24 and the preceding evening. In addition, certain students or staff
may be absent on one of the following holy days still remaining in this school
year: April 3 — Sikhs Baisakhi, May 2 — Greek Orthodox Holy Friday, and June 9
— Islamic Eid-Ul-Fita.

As you can appreciate, the development of a calendar such as
the one attached is an evolutionary process. In view of this, it is possible
that holy days of certain ethnocultural and religious groups may not be noted
on the calendar. Should you become aware of any such days please contact the
Public Relations Office such that these days might be included in future
calendars.

[
20
]

By letter dated February 8, 1994, the
Board received from the Acting Regional Director of the Ministry, a copy of a
letter from Imam Ahmad Kutty of the Islamic Foundation of Toronto drawing
attention to the observance of Ramadan and the festival Eid-al-Fitr. The letter
from the Ministry and the attached letter from Imam Kutty, were distributed by
the Board to all schools under its jurisdiction.

[
21
]

The letter from the Acting Regional
Director reads in part:

SUBJECT:
Ramadan and Eid-ul-Fitr

Together with this memorandum, please find a letter from Mr.
Ahmad Kutty, Imam, which provides information about the above two events which
are of great significance to the Muslim community. Staff and students who are
observing the fast and those who wish to pray, may need special accommodations.

Assisting all staff and students,
who wish to do so, in respect of the observances related to Ramadan and
Eid-au-Fitre is an important aspect of the system's antiracism and
ethnocultural equity education programs.

[
22
]

The lengthy two-page letter from Imam
Ahmad Kutty reads in part:

... We hope the following information is useful and helps
promote understanding and cooperation between the Muslim community and
educational institutions.

This year Ramadan will begin on the
weekend of February 12th and will continue through March 13th. ...

We are required to fast during the
month of Ramadan, ... by abstaining from food and drink from dawn to sunset. It
is a test of moral character, an education and an opportunity to meditate.

* * * * *

Muslim children attending schools
may be fasting during the month of Ramadan. We request staff in schools to
kindly keep in mind that the Muslim child may not be eating and drinking during
school hours and may be unable to participate in some physical activities.

... Also, some students may request
prayer facilities for about fifteen minutes daily between 12:30 - 1:00 p.m.
Efforts to accommodate these requests would be greatly appreciated.

We would also ask that this
important aspect of a Muslim child's life be shared with other children: with
teachers showing interest and asking questions about the child's fasting
routines.

The end of Ramadan is marked by
Eid-ul-Fitr, one of the major festivals in Islam. ... This year, Eid-ul-Fitr
(often shorted to just "Eid") will fall on March 13th or 14th, 1994.

* * * * *

This year's festival will take place
during the March break but we request that the date of Eid-ul-Fitr be marked on
school calendars as a Muslim holiday and that staff in schools recognize this
important event in their classes.

The Board's accommodation of Muslim students and their parents

[
23
]

Abdul-Kareem Abdul-Aziz, one of the
applicants by his litigation guardian, Sharon Fongenie, in 1993-94 was a
student enrolled under the name Kareem Fongenie at Laurentian High School, one
of the schools operated by the Board. However, he did not attend the school in
1994-95 because his family moved to Toronto. Students are not asked on
enrolment to indicate their religious affiliation. Bonnie Brake, the guidance
counsellor who worked with Kareem during 1993-94 because he asked for her
assistance, did not know he was of the Muslim faith. The subject of Kareem's
religion never came up on her many meetings with him and his mother. Brake,
during the year, helped Kareem with his study skills. When he had difficulty
with his tests, as a general rule he was given the opportunity to re-write
them. Brake feels that Kareem's difficulties were due in part to his failure to
fully comprehend English. According to Brake, when a student misses a test
because of a legitimate absence, such as for a holy day, the student is given
the opportunity to make up the test. In some courses where, for example, there
are 12 tests during a semester but only the best 10 tests are counted, it might
not be necessary to make up a missed test. Brake says that if Muslim students want
a classroom designated as a prayer room for the noon prayer, the school
obliges. In 1992-93, several Muslim students made a request for a prayer room
and a classroom was designated. In 1993-94, no students made such a request. In
the fall of 1994, four Muslim students asked for a prayer room and a classroom
was designated for that purpose.

[
24
]

Aysha Bassuny swore an affidavit on
September 8, 1994 in support of this application. She states in her affidavit
that there are approximately 200 Muslim students at Brookfield High School.
Neil Doherty, Principal of Brookfield High School, has sworn an affidavit in
support of the Board. He states that: Aysha Bassuny came to Brookfield in
September, 1993 for Grade 9 after having attended elementary school at the Ottawa
Islamic School in the City of Nepean; that the enrolment at Brookfield in
September, 1994 was approximately 1,100 pupils; that Bassuny's statement that
there are approximately 200 Muslim students at Brookfield is inaccurate; while
students are not asked upon enrolment to give their religious affiliation, 57
students indicated that their first language spoken is Arabic; that the number
of Muslim students in his estimation is fewer than 100; that students are not
penalized in any way for being absent from school to observe a religious holy
day. If the student misses a test through such absence, the student is given a
make-up test or the missed test is not counted in the overall evaluation of the
pupil. Mr. Doherty denies the allegation of Ms Bassuny that "the general
attitude among teachers and administrators in school is that such absence (i.e.
missing school on holy days) is equated with an unexcused absence from
school". Mr. Doherty swears that:

For the third year in a row I have permitted a group of young men
of the Islamic faith, with their prayer leader, to utilize a regular classroom
in the school over the noon hour for their midday prayers.

Last year I permitted Muslim students introduced by their
ESL/ESD teachers to make announcements over the public address system in
English and Arabic at the time of the Islamic faith observances. In addition, I
reserved the auditorium in the school for the entire student body to permit a
Muslim spokesperson to address the student body about the Islamic faith.

[
25
]

The Board, by a directive dated April
18, 1994, advised all schools of the observance by students of holy days and
attached a list of holy days designated by religious communities, including
Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha. It was specifically noted in this communication
that teachers should not schedule tests, exams or major co-curricular events on
such holy days.

[
26
]

In addition, commencing in 1993, the
Board has distributed multi-faith calendars to each school. These multi-faith
calendars contain an explanation of the holy days for the various world
religions, including Islam. The Board's practice in this respect is now being
followed by other school boards in Ontario.

[
27
]

Starting in 1990, the Board established
a policy under which meetings of the Board and its committees would not take
place on holy days. That policy specifically provides that representatives of
the religions which are practised in the Board's jurisdiction will be requested
to advise the Board as to their holy days so that the Board may schedule its
meetings accordingly.

[
28
]

In 1979, the Board created a
Multiculturalism Advisory Committee to provide advice on matters of concern to
the ethnocultural communities in the Ottawa area. The Multiculturalism Advisory
Committee acts as a two-way link between the Board and ethno-cultural
communities, including the Muslim community. Members articulate and communicate
views, interests and concerns of their ethno-cultural communities and, at the
same time, keep such communities informed of the policies, decisions, programs and
activities of the Board. This Committee usually meets monthly.

[
29
]

In 1984, the Board developed a written
policy on racism and ethnic relations. The preamble or introduction to that
written policy document states in part:

... every child has the right to an education, free from
racial or ethnic bias, which will enable the child to participate as fully as
possible in the larger Canadian community. With the rapid growth of adult
education programs and the concept of life long learning it is equally
important that the same be true for the adult learner. It is the responsibility
of the school system to include among its learning opportunities those which
will enable the student to acquire knowledge and to develop attitudes and
values which will further the elimination of racial and ethnic discrimination
from our society.

[
30
]

The Board also operates heritage
language classes which include the Arabic-Iraqi School, the Somali Heritage
Language School and the Arabic-Egyptian School. Representatives of these
schools serve on the Multiculturalism Advisory Committee.

[
31
]

It is the opinion of the Director of
Education for the Board that having regard to the long established practices of
the Board, the existence of the Multiculturalism Advisory Committee and the
Anti-Racism and Ethno-Cultural Equity Policies that the cultural and religious
divergence of students and staff, has been fully recognized and supported by
the Board.

Establishment of the 1994-95 School Year

[
32
]

For many years, consultations have been
held with teachers, labour unions and administrators through the mechanism of
the School Year Calendar Committee in preparing the annual recommendation for
the Board on the school year. On September 28, 1993, the Superintendent of
Human Resources sent to the Calendar Committee members a memorandum which
contained a proposed school calendar schedule for 1994-95. This proposed
calendar followed the five-year Ministry school year and school holidays
instructions, but he pointed out to the committee members that in 1994 Rosh
Hashanah occurred on Tuesday, September 6 and Wednesday, September 7, 1994.

[
33
]

On January 31, 1994, the Director of
Education for the Board received a letter from Ron Singer, Community Relations
Chairperson, Jewish Community Council of Ottawa, requesting an accommodation for
the Jewish students and teachers who would be absent from school during Rosh
Hashanah which fell on September 6 and 7, 1994. Mr. Singer wrote again on
February 15, 1994 advising that such an accommodation was being considered in
Metro Toronto and of discussions between the Ministry and the Canadian Jewish
Congress.

[
34
]

On March 21, 1994, the question of the
1994-95 school year came before the Board's Human Resources Committee. At that
time, Mr. Singer appeared and made a submission on the possibility of adjusting
the starting date for school to September 8, 1994 because of Rosh Hashanah. He
pointed out that missing the first two days of school would place the Jewish
students in a position of being unnecessarily disoriented as they are being
integrated into the classroom, particularly those starting their first year in
a new school. This would include such problems as the assignment of lockers,
issuing of class schedules, and learning materials. Mr. Singer noted that the
coincidence of Rosh Hashanah with the beginning of the school year was an
extremely unusual event not likely to occur again for three or four decades. At
the same meeting of the Human Resources Committee a report from the School Year
Calendar Committee was submitted as well as correspondence from the Jewish
Community Council of Ottawa and from other Toronto area school boards. The
Human Resources Committee referred this report back to senior administration
for further consideration.

[
35
]

On March 23, 1994, the Multicultural
Advisory Committee passed a resolution recommending that classes should begin
on Thursday, September 8, 1994, that September 7 be a school-based P.A. day and
that June 30, 1995 be the last day of school.

[
36
]

On or about March 31, 1994, the Board
received a letter from the National Capital Alliance on Race Relations
recommending the respondent adjust its school calendar so that the first day of
classes be on September 8, 1994 as September 6 and 7 were high holy days of the
Jewish faith.

[
37
]

After a further meeting of the School
Year Calendar Committee, the Director of Education submitted a report to the
trustees. It set forth the various options for the school year calendar for
1994-95 and recognized that the coincidence of the holy day and the opening of
the academic year was "a rare and infrequent event".

[
38
]

At the regular Board meeting on April
11, 1994, a resolution was adopted whereby the beginning of the 1994-95 school
year would be September 7, 1994 as a professional activity day; that September
8, 1994 be the starting date for school for students; and that the last day of
school be June 30, 1995.

[
39
]

On April 12, 1994, the Board's school
year calendar for 1994-95 was sent to the Ministry for approval. On or about
April 15, 1994, the Board received Ministry approval for the 1994-95 school
year.

Request by the Islamic Schools Federation of Ontario and the
Ottawa-Carleton Muslim Association for School Holidays to celebrate Eid-al-Fitr
and Eid-al-Adha

[
40
]

By a letter dated April 19, 1994,
signed by the President, Ottawa Muslim Association and the Chairman, Islamic
Schools Federation of Ontario, the Board was commended for delaying the opening
of the school year to accommodate Rosh Hashanah and was requested to
"extend the decision to include other religion components" including
the Muslim holy days of Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha. This was the first request
received by the Board from the Muslim community. This issue had not been
previously raised in the meetings of the Multicultural Advisory Committee on
which Committee, as indicated above, the Muslim community is represented. The
letter of April 19, 1994 reads in part:

You may be interested to know that according to census 1991
(see attached), the population of Muslims living in Ottawa-Hull area was 17,585
of whom there were young people ages 1 to 24. Assuming that 13 out of 24 of
this age group went to school, it is estimated that the number of students in
Ottawa-Hull was 4,680. Deducting 180 students attended a private Islamic school
and assuming that one half of the rest attended OBE schools, the number of
Muslim students in the OBE schools stands at 2250.

Using the same source of information and the methodology of
calculation, the number of Jewish students in the OBE schools will stand at 410
and not 1500 as has been reported in the Citizen.

[
41
]

On April 25, 1994, Mr. Qasem Mahmud
appeared before the Board on behalf of the Islamic Schools Federation of
Ontario and requested that schools be closed on March 3 and May 11, 1995
because of the two Muslim holy days and that these days be used as professional
activity days. At the same meeting a presentation was made by Abdul Sattar
Bhatti of the Ottawa Muslim Association who asked that the Board establish a
committee to study the issue. The Board took no action on these requests.

[
42
]

On April 29, 1994, Emilio S. Binavince,
counsel for the applicants, wrote the Board in part as follows:

Re:
Islamic Holidays
—
Academic
Year 1994/95

I act on behalf of the Islamic
School Federation of Ontario, Ottawa Muslim Association, and their parents and
students who are currently attending schools in the Board's jurisdiction.

I understand that the request of my
clients for school holidays on March 3 and 4, 1995 (Eidulfitr), and May 11,
1995 (Eiduladha), sacred holidays in the Islamic religion, has not been decided
upon by the Board. I write this letter to request you to provide us with your
decision on or before Monday, May 16, 1994. If, by this date, my clients are
not in receipt of a decision on this matter, they will assume that their
request has been rejected.

As you know, the request has been
made not to challenge the holidays of other religions but simply for equal
treatment of these two religious Islamic holidays. The recognition of holidays
of the Jewish community is a step in the right direction and should be extended
to these Islamic holidays. As you probably know, there are approximately four
times the number of Muslim students to Jewish students in the OBE. The refusal
to recognise these two holidays may be a breach of religious freedom and may
constitute discrimination which could be challenged in the courts.

[
43
]

On May 3, 1994, Mr. Binavince sent a
second letter correcting an error in the first. The second letter reads in
part:

... May I correct this error and also confirm that the
holidays are as follows:

(a) March 3, 1995- Eidulfitr; and

(b) May 11, 1995 — Eiduladha.

Thank you for your indulgence.

[
44
]

On May 4, 1994, the Board answered Mr.
Binavince by letter which reads in part:

... When the Ottawa Board of Education considered the request
from the Jewish community to delay the start of the 1994-95 school year, the
issue before the Board was not the recognition of the holy days of the Jewish
faith but rather an opening of school issue and how best to accommodate the
children of the Jewish community who would be disadvantaged by not being able
to participate in the opening exercises. Teachers and administrators outlined
the problems in helping these students if they missed the first two days of
school and the Board, as well as other school boards in this province, felt
that this was one way of responding to the situation. At no time, was
consideration given to the merits of recognizing religious holy days in the
school year calendar, as this Board respects all religions present in our
school system today and tries to respond in every way in making the school
system respectful of the different religious practices followed by the students
and the parents in our community.

I would like to, once again, emphasize that the adjustment
made to the school year for this coming September was looked upon as a one-time
event and not as a precedent for readjusting the academic school year on an
ongoing basis.

I hope this information is satisfactory to your needs. We will
continue to try to accommodate the needs of all our students. It should also be
understood that the Ottawa Board of Education has always been respectful of the
rights of the children to be away on the special holy days of their religious
faith and, in addition, the absence of teachers on holy days is recognized in
the collective agreements.

[
45
]

On May 12, 1994, Mr. Binavince wrote to
the Board in part as follows:

... characterising the issue relating to the Jewish
community's request, not as a recognition of a Jewish holiday, but rather the
opening of the school year, is nice but meaningless; however one characterises
it, they amount to the same-thing. The fact remains that the opening of the
school year falls on a Jewish holiday and the opening was postponed by the
Board because of the Jewish community's request.

[
46
]

On May 16, 1994, the Board wrote to Mr.
Binavince as follows:

I acknowledge receipt of your letter of May 12, 1994 in which
you claim that the request of your client to the Ottawa Board of Education has
been ignored. The Ottawa Board of Education has not ignored the response to your
client and my letter of May 3, 1994 tried to represent the position of the
Board on the issue of the recognition of sacred holidays in the school
calendar.

I appreciate that you do not accept the position of the Board
as stated in my previous letter, however, that letter does represent the
position of the Board on this issue.

[
47
]

The Board, because of concern about the
cost of legal proceedings, considered the matter further at its meeting on June
13, 1994 but decided not to change its previous decision of April 11, 1994 with
respect to the school year.

The Arguments of the Applicants and My Disposition of Them

[
48
]

The Board was asked (1) to make one
or both of the Muslim high holy days of Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha, which
would fall on Friday, March 3 and Thursday, May 11 respectively, school
holidays for the 1994-95 school year, and (2) to study the issue of holy days
of the various religions and to consider ways to accommodate such holy days in
the school calendar.

[
49
]

I point out, though it perhaps makes
little difference, that the actual request made of the Board was that it create
school holidays for both Muslim holy days. When Qasem Mahmud appeared before
the Board on April 25, 1994, he requested that the schools be closed on March 3
and May 11, 1995 and suggested that professional development days could be
scheduled for those days so as to allow holidays to be extended to all the
Board's schools.

[
50
]

In any event, the applicants make this
argument. The refusal of the Board to create school holidays for one or both of
the Islamic holy days, in the face of the accommodation of the Christian holy
days of Christmas, Good Friday and Easter Monday, and of the two Jewish holy
days of Rosh Hashanah constitutes discrimination, contrary to
s. 15
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
It is said that the Muslims asked only for
the same consideration that was given to the Jewish students. Further, it is
said that the recognition by Regulation 304 of Christian holy days by making
them school holidays infringes the guarantee of freedom of conscience and
religion contained in
section 2(
a
) of the
Charter.

Disposition

[
51
]

I point out that Easter Monday is not a
Christian holy day. It is like the day after Christmas, boxing day, a day for
recuperation. While Good Friday is with Christmas and Easter, one of the three
most significant days in the Christian calendar, there is no evidence before us
that it is a Christian holy day. At least in the Roman Catholic church, apart
from Sundays, there are now only two holy days — Christmas Day and New Year's
Day. While services are held on Good Friday in Christian churches, attendance
at those services is not obligatory. Though there is no evidence on the point,
I suspect very few of the Board's Christian children attend those services. My
point is that most Christian children could attend school on Good Friday and
Easter Monday without offending their conscience.

[
52
]

Christmas and Easter are of course
different. The faithful are expected to observe them. But no attention is paid
by the applicants to Easter, presumably because it always falls on a Sunday and
so would be a school holiday in any event. Which brings me to the contention of
the applicants, that some of the school holidays provided for in the
Education
Act
are for observance of Christian holy days. Such argument is no longer
tenable. It has been laid to rest by decisions of both the Court of Appeal for
Ontario and the Supreme Court of Canada.

[
53
]

In
R. v. Edwards Books and Art Ltd.
,

1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
,
[1986] 2 S.C.R. 713
at 746-47,
35 D.L.R. (4th) 1
, Dickson C.J. after concluding
that the
Ontario
Retail Business Holidays Act
which prohibited retail
stores, with some exceptions, being open for business on Sundays, had as its
object the allowance of as many people as possible to enjoy a secular weekly
common pause day as recommended by the Ontario Law Reform Commission, then
quoted from the
Report on Sunday Observance Legislation
that the
Commission had produced:

"Sunday as a day of religious observance in Ontario
appears to be decreasing in significance, if church and Sunday school
attendance on that day is any indication. But this does not mean that Sunday is
losing its significance as a pause day — characterized by a high degree of
social interaction and leisure activities among family and friends. Indeed, our
behavioural research revealed that Sunday in Ontario in 1970 has these latter
characteristics to a very high degree, certainly more so than on any other day
of the week. We would therefore regard the singling out of Sunday as the day of
government support as consistent with the promotion of these characteristics.
[pp. 268-69]

* * * * *

"There are very few countries in the world in which
Sunday has not been chosen as the uniform pause day by legislation. Yet many of
these countries would hardly characterize their legislation as
"Christian" or "religious" in nature. The U.S.S.R., for
example, established Sunday as the pause day (or "day off") by an
edict of the Praesidium of the Supreme Soviet in 1940. We were told by the
Canadian Ambassador in Moscow that Sunday is officially a day of rest,
recreation, cultural education, amusement and political activity. The basic
labour law of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia recognizes Sunday as
a day of rest subject to municipal regulation, and violations of municipal
ordinances respecting Sunday work are subject to fines. Even in Japan, a country
where Christianity has never been more than a minor religion, three separate
government regulations exist requiring Sunday to be a day of rest, the first
promulgated in 1876 relating to public servants, the second in 1922 relating to
business hours at government agencies, and the third in 1949 respecting the
1922 regulation and adding that officials should be on duty every day except
holidays and Sundays. We were advised by the Canadian Ambassador in Japan that
Sunday is not a working day except for people in service industries and retail
merchandising, but neither is it a day of religious observance.

"In short, there are sufficient precedents throughout the
world for legislative selection of Sunday as a uniform pause day for
secular

rather than
religious
purposes. For the reasons outlined, we would
propose that this practice be followed in Ontario. [pp. 269-70]"

Dickson C.J. then stated at p. 747:

The Report concedes at p. 269 that the selection of Sunday as
a pause day would have the incidental effect of benefiting a substantial
minority of the population that attends church on Sundays. I am satisfied,
however, that acknowledgment of the religious effects of a Sunday pause day is
precisely that: a frank acknowledgment of
effects
, rather than an expression
of concealed
purpose.

Finally, at p. 752, Dickson C.J. stated:

The Act has a secular purpose which is not offensive to the
Charter

guarantee of freedom of conscience and religion.

[
54
]

Dickson C.J. then explored whether the
impugned Act interfered by its effects with freedom of conscience and religion
guaranteed by
s. 2
(a)
of the
Charter
, for "[i]t matters not,
... whether a coercive burden is direct or indirect, intentional or
unintentional, foreseeable or unforeseeable. All coercive burdens on the
exercise of religious beliefs are potentially within the ambit of
s.
2
(a)." But "[f]or a state-imposed cost or burden to be proscribed by

s. 2
(
a
), it must be capable of interfering with religious belief or
practice"
(per
Dickson C.J. at p. 759).

[
55
]

Some Christians consider Sunday holy
and abide the commandment "Remember that thou keep holy the Sabbath
day." The
Retail Business Holidays Act
is consistent with such a
religious belief and practice. But according to Dickson C.J. at p. 760,
"One is not being compelled to engage in religious practices merely
because a statutory obligation coincides with the dictates of a particular
religion" and, at p. 761, "legislation with a secular inspiration
does not abridge the freedom from conformity to religious dogma merely because
statutory provisions coincide with the tenets of a religion".

[
56
]

The
Retail Business Holidays Act

did not then force anyone to conform to Christian religious dogma.

[
57
]

But did the Act have an impact that
significantly infringed on the freedom to manifest or practise religious
beliefs? Dickson C.J. concluded that the
Retail Business Holidays Act
, exemptions
aside, has the effect of making it more costly for some Jewish and Seventh Day
Adventist retailers to practise their religious beliefs and that accordingly their
freedom of religion is abridged by the Act.

[
58
]

Dickson C.J. then considered whether
such abridgment is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society. At p. 769 he states:

I will address, first, the importance of the legislative objectives
underlying the
Retail Business Holidays Act
.
The Ontario Law Reform
Commission referred to the need for legislation enacting a uniform pause day in
the following terms at p. 267:

"Thus while our productive capacity and economic standard
of living continue to increase in Ontario, our collective opportunity for the
more intangible benefits of participating in leisure activities
together

[emphasis of the Report] with family, friends and others in society continues
to decrease. It is in the light of this continuing erosion of statutory
holidays and evening hours that we consider it
absolutely essential
[emphasis
added] that the government now attempt to preserve at least one uniform day
each week as a pause day, before it is too late."

... I regard as self-evident the desirability of enabling
parents to have regular days off from work in common with their child's day off
from school, and with a day off enjoyed by most other family and community
members. I reiterate the view expressed in
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.
, at p.
353:

"I accept the secular justification for a day of rest in
a Canadian context and the reasonableness of a day of rest has been clearly
enunciated by the courts in the United States of America."

A family visit to an uncle or a grandmother, the attendance of
a parent at a child's sports tournament, a picnic, a swim, or a hike in the
park on a summer day, or a family expedition to a zoo, circus, or exhibition —
these, and hundreds of other leisure activities with family and friends are
amongst the simplest but most profound joys that any of us can know. The aim of
protecting workers, families and communities from a diminution of opportunity
to experience the fulfilment offered by these activities, and from the
alienation of the individual from his or her closest social bonds, is not one
which I regard as unimportant or trivial. In the context of the
"fast-growing trend toward wide-scale store openings" (Report, p.
267), I am satisfied that the Act is aimed at a pressing and substantial concern.
It therefore survives the first part of the inquiry under s. 1.

[
59
]

As to whether the means chosen by the
legislature to ensure a common pause day is proportional to that purpose or
end, Dickson C.J. states at p. 772:

... the resultant legislation need not be tuned with great
precision in order to withstand judicial scrutiny. Simplicity and
administrative convenience are legitimate concerns for the drafters of such
legislation.

A more difficult question — and one which goes to the heart of
this litigation — is whether the
Retail Business Holidays Act
abridges
the freedom of religion on Saturday observers as little as is reasonably
possible.

At pages 778-9, Dickson C.J. states:

What cannot be forgotten is that the object of the legislation
is to benefit retail employees by making available to them a weekly holiday
which coincides with that enjoyed by most of the community.

* * * * *

I cannot fault the Legislature for determining that the
protection of the employees ought to prevail.

[
60
]

I now turn to the
Peel (Regional Municipality)
v. Great Atlantic & Pacific Co. of Canada Ltd.

(1991),
1991 CanLII 7068 (ON CA)
,
2 O.R. (3d) 65
,

78 D.L.R. (4th) 333 (C.A.)
in which the constitutionality of the
Retail
Business Holidays Act
as amended in 1989 was the issue. Dubin C.J.O. stated
at pages 78-80:

New Year's Day, Good Friday,
Christmas Day and December 26

In the Act, as amended, the
above-mentioned days are included in the definition of "holiday". It
was on this basis alone that Southey J. held that the Act limited the freedom
of religion of non-Christian retailers by reason of being compelled to close on
those days.

* * * * *

It is first to be observed that
"New Year's Day", "Good Friday" and "Christmas
Day" were also included in the definition of "holiday" under the
Act before amendment, and "December 26" has now been substituted for
what was described as "Boxing Day" in the unamended Act. It is not
without significance that the inclusion of these days in the Act was not held
to be an abridgment of the guarantee of freedom of religion of Saturday
non-Christian observers when the constitutionality of the Act was considered in
the
Videoflicks, Edwards Books
and
Paul Magder Furs
cases.

In concluding that the Act was
secular and not intended to enforce or encourage religious observance, Chief
Justice Dickson in
Edwards Books
stated as follows at pp. 742-44 S.C.R.,
pp. 21-22 C.R.R.:

"... distinctive legislative treatment of a day, such as
Sunday, which has particular religious significance does not invariably require
the legislation to be characterized as religious in nature. It is upon this
second point that I now wish to dwell.

"It is beyond doubt that days
such as Sundays, Christmas and Easter were celebrated as holidays in Canada
historically for religious reasons. The celebration of these holidays has
continued to the present partly because of continuing, though diminished,
religious observances of the largest denominations of the Christian faith,
partly because of statutory enforcement under,
inter alia
, the now
unconstitutional
Lord's Day Act
, and partly because of the combined
effect of social inertia and the perceived need for people to have days away
from work or school in common with family, friends and other members of the
community. These, in my view, are the social facts which explain the selection
by individuals, businesses, school boards, and others of particular days as
holidays.

"It is important to keep in
mind, however, that the Court is not called upon to characterize the historical
origins or even the continuing cause for the selection by individual members of
the community of particular holidays. To do so would be to characterize social
facts rather than characterizing the impugned law. The question in the present
cases therefore cannot be reduced to a mathematical exercise of computing the
number of holidays prescribed by the Act which have a religious origin. Our
society is collectively powerless to repudiate its history, including the
Christian heritage of the majority.

* * * * *

"What therefore emerges is the
question of whether it can be said that the impugned statute has for its true
object, purpose and character, the prevention of the profanation of Sunday or
other days of religious significance, or whether it is designed to provide
holidays for some persons engaged in certain retail trades.

"An examination of the statute
itself and the agreed statement of facts does not reveal a legislative object
or intent to prevent the profanation of the Sabbath or other days of religious
significance. On the contrary, the title of the enactment and its substantive
provisions reveals that the Legislature desired and intended to make provisions
for holidays to some persons engaged in certain retail trades. The fact that
Sunday and some other days of a religious significance are included in the
definition of "holiday" is incidental to the main purpose of the
legislation and is not a sufficient basis from which to conclude that the
statute is directed towards the prevention of the profanation of the Sabbath or
other days of religious significance and thus beyond provincial legislative
competence."

With respect, I think Southey J. erred in defining Good Friday
and Christmas Day, as well as the others, as religious holidays in the context
of the
Retail Business Holidays Act
.
Although admittedly Good Friday and
Christmas Day are also observed for religious reasons, in modern society they
must be viewed as secular common pause days. The fact that a day selected for a
common pause day coincides with a day which is a religious holiday for some
does not, in my opinion, render that selection unconstitutional.

As I emphasized above [quoting from
Edwards Books
, p.
759 S.C.R., p. 34 C.R.R.]:

"Section 2
(a)
does not require the legislatures to
eliminate every minuscule state-imposed cost associated with the practice of
religion."

In my opinion, if the selection of Good Friday and Christmas
Day as two of the common pause days limits the freedom of religion of those
retailers who do not observe those days as their religious holidays, such limit
would be trivial and insubstantial and would not be protected by
s.
2(a)

of the
Charter
.

[
61
]

If Sundays, Good Friday and Christmas
are secular common pause days for the purposes of the
Retail Business
Holidays Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. R.30, then in the absence of evidence that
they were named as school holidays because of their religious significance,
those days and Saturday and Easter Monday as well are secular holidays and not
religious holy days under Regulation 304. There is no evidence and there is
nothing in Regulation 304 to suggest those days are anything but secular common
pause days, and that is what I find them to be.

[
62
]

Nevertheless, the applicants allege
that part of the purpose of Regulation 304 is to celebrate or allow for the
celebration of certain Christian holy days. Objection is taken to only
paragraphs 5, 7 and 8 of section 2(4) of Regulation 304 which reads in part:

2(4) Subject to section 5, the following are school holidays:

1. Every Saturday and Sunday.

* * * * *

5. A Christmas vacation consisting of fourteen consecutive
days commencing on the Monday next following the Friday preceding the 21st day
of December, but when the 21st day of December is a Thursday or a Friday,
commencing on the Monday next following.

7. Good Friday.

8. Easter Monday.

[
63
]

Counsel for the applicants stated
before us that he was not pushing his attack on paragraph 5 very hard because
the paragraph itself speaks of the 14 day break at Christmas as being a
vacation and because Christmas has taken on a secular nature. But he maintained
that Good Friday and Easter Monday are Christian holy days that have not been
secularized.

[
64
]

There is before us no evidence that
Easter Monday has ever been recognized as a holy day in Ontario. We are told by
the applicant that prior to 1954:

The earlier legislation did not specifically list the school
year holidays, but rather, referred to public or statutory holidays, which were
defined in the provincial Interpretations Acts. The definition of
"holiday" in the Interpretation Act can be traced back to the
earliest Canadian
Interpretation Act
of 1849 (12 Vic. C. 10, s. 5(12).

I note, however, that Section V of the
Interpretation Act
,
S.C. 1849, c. 10, reads in part:

Twelfthly.
The word "holiday" shall include
Sundays, New Years Day, the Epiphany, the Annunciation, Good-Friday, the
Ascension,
Corpus Christi
, St. Peter and St. Paul's Day, all Saints Day
and Christmas Day, — and any day appointed by Proclamation for a General Fast or
Thanksgiving.

[
65
]

While it can be said that the days
mentioned were Christian holy days, Easter Monday was not one of them.

[
66
]

It must be remembered that until a
relatively few years ago, the school year provided for Easter holidays as well
as Christmas holidays. The Easter holidays commenced on Good Friday and ended
the Sunday after Easter. When provision was made for a fixed March break, the
lengthy Easter holidays were reduced to four days. There is no evidence that
the four day Easter holiday was retained to accommodate Christian holy days. It
appears rather those days were retained as holidays to provide for common pause
or rest days to coincide with holidays enjoyed by much of the business
community.

[
67
]

In short, other than the use of the
words "Good Friday", "Christmas" and "Easter",
the applicants point to nothing that indicates that the school holidays
enumerated in s. 2(4) of Regulation 304 have any religious significance. Any
religious significance that arises from the names only can also be found in the
words "Saturday" and "Sunday" found in s. 2(4), para. 1
which are also named as school holidays. The use of words that have religious
significance does not establish that holidays declared for those days were so
declared to allow religious observance of those days.

[
68
]

I am satisfied that on the evidence and
on the law, the school holidays named in s. 2(4) of Regulation 304 that are
impugned are common pause days or rest days that have been chosen to coincide
with holidays or pause days enjoyed by society generally.

[
69
]

Neither the legislature nor anyone else
can deny our history and remove religious significance from Saturday and
Sunday, Christmas, Good Friday and Easter. But the legislature was entitled to
create school holidays and make those holidays coincide with common pause
holidays and rest days enjoyed by society generally. By making the school
holidays coincide with the common pause days and holidays prescribed in other
legislation for society generally, the legislature was accepting a reality,
that our society generally has come to accept as secular holidays — Saturday,
Sunday, Christmas and Easter holidays. There is no obligation on the
legislature to disrupt and reorganize these rest days and holidays because some
of them fall on days some consider holy days. Indeed, it would be a practical
impossibility to do so. Consider, for example, that Sunday is recognized over
much of the world as a day of rest, even in countries that are not
predominantly Christian. Ontario could not change our common weekly rest days
from Saturday and Sunday to, say, Monday and Tuesday. Our stock market and
business generally could not operate on such a schedule. The same applies with
less dramatic effect to any attempt to change the Christmas holidays so as to
exclude Christmas Day. Ontario would be out of step with the rest of the
western world, and would suffer all the disruption to business and pleasure
being so out of step would entail. The same applies to the short Easter
vacation.

[
70
]

Since Regulation 304 creates secular
holidays, the purpose or object of the regulation does not violate the
guarantee of freedom of conscience and religion found in
s. 2(
a
) of the
Charter
,
nor the right given by
s. 15
of the
Charter
to equal benefit of the law
without discrimination.

[
71
]

But does Regulation 304 by its effects
interfere with either of those rights?

[
72
]

In my view, Regulation 304 does not
have the effect of infringing the Muslims' freedom of religion. As already
indicated, by virtue of
s. 21(2)
of the
Education Act
, "a child is
excused from attendance at school if ...
(g)
the child is absent on a
day regarded as a holy day by the church or religious denomination to which the
child belongs". If a Muslim holy day falls on a school day, the child can
stay away from school. The fact a parent may have to sign a note confirming
that the child missed school because of the holy day is surely not onerous nor
an infringement of freedom of religion. Some explanation is required when a
student is absent for any reason. I do not accept that in a multi-cultural
society there should be any embarrassment or alienation surrounding either
taking the day off school or tendering a note to the school explaining it. This
is especially so where, as here, the Muslim students ask for and are given a
room in which to pray at noon, make announcements over the public address
system concerning Muslim religious events and exercises and where Muslim groups
encourage the teachers and the students to become familiar with the tenets of
the Muslim faith, its practices and holy days. But if there be some
embarrassment or tension, it is caused not by the legislation which is secular,
but by the fact the student's religion requires him to miss school.

[
73
]

As was stated by Dickson C.J. in
Edwards
Books, supra
, at p. 759:

The purpose of s. 2
(a)
is to ensure that society does
not interfere with profoundly personal beliefs that govern one's perception of
oneself, humankind, nature, and, in some cases, a higher or different order of
being. These beliefs, in turn, govern one's conduct and practices. The
Constitution shelters individuals and groups only to the extent that religious
beliefs or conduct might reasonably or actually be threatened. For a
state-imposed cost or burden to be proscribed by
s. 2
(a)
it must be
capable of interfering with religious belief or practice.

[
74
]

Since Regulation 304 creates secular
holidays, it cannot be said that it forces Muslims to observe Christian holy
days. Because the
Education Act
excuses a student from attendance at
school on his holy days, the Act does not require a student to violate his
religious belief. Regulation 304 does not then infringe freedom of religion in
its purpose or its effect.

[
75
]

But does Regulation 304 create adverse
effect discrimination?

[
76
]

There is no evidence on this
application as to what percentage of Christian students attending the schools
of the Ottawa Board actually attend church services on Christmas Day or Good
Friday, or would consider it a violation of their conscience if they were
required to attend school on those days. The supposed benefit to Christian
students in having school holidays coincide with certain Christian holy days
may be more apparent than real.

[
77
]

Suppose a full investigation were to
disclose that only 15% of students go to church on Christmas Day and only 2%
attend church on Good Friday, and suppose as well that 90% of Christian
students would not consider it violated their conscience or their religious
beliefs to attend classes on either day. Would the applicants still maintain
that Christians benefitted by not having to miss school as the Muslims do on
their holy days?

[
78
]

I doubt it would be proper to make a
finding of adverse effect discrimination on the evidence available on this
application.

[
79
]

The applicants point to
CSR de Chambly
v. Bergevin, supra
where the Supreme Court of Canada found adverse effect
discrimination in the fact Jewish teachers working for a Public Board in Quebec
had to take a day off work without pay to celebrate Yom Kippur, whereas the
Christian teachers did not have to take time off to observe their holy days
because the Christian holy days fell on school holidays. I point out there is a
vast difference between the likely observance of holy days by Christian
teachers in the Catholic system in Quebec, and the observance of holy days by
Christian students of the Ottawa Board.

[
80
]

I must say that I agree with Finlayson
J.A. when he said
in
Peel (Regional Municipality)
, supra
at p. 104-5:

There is something unrealistic about treating the named
holidays in the Act as Christian religious holidays. It presupposes that the
majority of the population are adherents to this religion and confine their
activities on these days to religious observance and nothing else. You must
accept this as a premise before you can set against it the circumstances of
minoritarian non-Sunday observers who, in addition to being forbidden by their
religion from shopping on their holy days, are prevented by the Act from
shopping on the Christian holidays. In order to show that one is being treated
differently, one must establish in relation to whom one receives different
treatment. Otherwise there is no relative discrimination. The non-Christians
cannot contend that they suffer discrimination under the Act by reason of their
religion unless there is some significant advantage to Christians, amounting to
more than convenience, in having their sabbath and the pause day coincide. But
nowhere in the record is there any evidence as to the number of Christians who
do not shop on Sunday because of their religious beliefs.

[
81
]

Nevertheless, I am prepared to deal
with this application, making the assumption that there is adverse effect
discrimination resulting from the fact that the Muslim students must take two
days off from school because of Muslim holy days while Christian students do
not have to miss any time because of their holy days.

[
82
]

In that event, I must consider whether
the infringement caused by Regulation 304 to the Muslims' right to equal
protection and benefit of the law without discrimination is justified under
s.
1
of the
Charter
.
Section 1 reads:

1. The
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
guarantees
the rights and freedoms set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits
prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic
society.

[
83
]

The criteria I must address in considering
the matter are summarized by Dickson C.J. in
Edwards Books, supra
, at p.
768:

It has been held that the onus of proof is on the party
seeking the limitation, and the standard of proof is the civil standard, proof
by a preponderance of probabilities.

Two requirements must be satisfied to establish that a limit
is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
First, the legislative objective which the limitation is designed to promote
must be of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a constitutional right.
It must bear on a "pressing and substantial concern". Second, the
means chosen to attain those objectives must be proportional or appropriate to
the ends. The proportionality requirement, in turn, normally has three aspects:
the limiting measures must be carefully designed, or rationally connected, to
the objective; they must impair the right as little as possible; and their
effects must not so severely trench on individual or group rights that the
legislative objective, albeit important, is nevertheless outweighed by the
abridgment of rights.

[
84
]

I should point out that the applicants
attack paragraphs 5, 7 and 8 of s. 2(4) of Regulation 304 solely on the grounds
that the purpose of those paragraphs is to provide holidays for the observance
of the alleged Christian holy days of Christmas Day, Good Friday and Easter
Monday. Of course, I have found such is not the purpose of those paragraphs,
rather it is to provide for secular holidays. The applicants did not make the
argument that if Regulation 304 has a valid and neutral purpose, it
nevertheless, by its effect, offends the Muslims' freedom of religion and
freedom from discrimination guaranteed by the
Charter
.
The applicants
did not therefore argue that Regulation 304 could not be justified under
s. 1

of the
Charter.
Not having the benefit of argument on the point, I will
deal with it briefly.

[
85
]

No one would question the need for
school holidays or doubt they are so vital to the learning process as to
warrant overriding a constitutional right. Further, the creation of those
holidays filled what would have been a pressing and substantial concern if they
had not been created. Regulation 304 survives then the first part of the
inquiry under s. 1.

[
86
]

The legislature or the government as
far as possible has chosen school holidays that coincide with the holidays
specified for in other legislation that creates secular common pause or rest
days for the community at large. There are of course more school holidays than
there are holidays in say the
Retail Business Holidays Act
, but all the
holidays provided for in the
Retail Business Holidays Act
are also made
school holidays by Regulation 304. In particular, Christmas Day and Good Friday
are school holidays that are also provided for in the
Retail Business
Holidays Act.

[
87
]

It seems to me that in choosing school
holidays that can be enjoyed by students and parents in common with the rest of
the community, the legislature interfered the least it could with the holy days
celebrated by various religions. The applicants did argue that if school
holidays could not be declared for the Muslim holy days, then certain portions
of Regulation 304 should be struck down. It was not suggested, however, that
some days other than Christmas and Good Friday would be more convenient
holidays. For both convenience and necessity, so Ontario may fit in with the
rest of the western world, Christmas and Good Friday must remain school
holidays.

[
88
]

I conclude, therefore, that the school
holidays chosen are appropriate ones to meet the needs of the students and
interfere as little as possible with the holy days of various religions. The
only way adverse effect discrimination could be avoided would be to make every
holy day of every student into a holiday. Even if that were possible, the new
legislation would be invalid. Such legislation would provide for religious not
secular holidays. The closing of schools for the celebration of religious holy
days would be contrary to the
Charter
.
Atheists, agnostics and those not
affiliated with any religious denomination would have a legitimate complaint
that their rights to a sensible and convenient school calendar were being
sacrificed in the interest of religion. According to the 1991 census, while
almost 2% of those living in the Ottawa-Hull region are Islamic, more than 12%
of the population of Canada have no religious affiliations. I conclude,
therefore, that to the extent that Regulation 304 infringes the Muslims' right
to equal benefit of the law, such infringement is a reasonable limitation on
that right that can be and is demonstrably justified in a free and democratic
society. Regulation 304 does not infringe the
Charter.

[
89
]

Even though Regulation 304 is valid, I
will assume that the Board, or indeed the Ministry, has an obligation to take
reasonable steps to accommodate the Muslims so as to undo the harm, namely two
days missed from school, caused by the discrimination. I have already pointed
out why it would not be feasible to attempt to change the Christmas and Easter
holidays, and in that way eliminate the discrimination complained of — that is
to say, by removing the alleged advantage Christians receive by having their
holy days on holidays.

[
90
]

The applicants base their argument that
the two most important Muslim holy days should be recognized as school
holidays, on the fact that Muslims comprise a substantial proportion of the
pupils in the schools of the Ottawa Board. I fail to appreciate why the numbers
of Muslims makes any difference. It seems to me that the same disadvantage will
be felt by any student who has a religious holy day that must be observed and
that does not fall on a school holiday. That disadvantage will not increase
because many share that same holy day. Any obligation to relieve such disadvantage
must apply to all who suffer it, not just to large groups who suffer it.

[
91
]

But for the fact it would be contrary
to the
Charter
, the surest way to relieve against such a disadvantage
would be to declare a new school holiday for every pupil who has such a holy
day. That, however, is impossible. There are only two or three days available
(depending on the day of the week on which September 1 falls) between September
1 and June 30. The rest are accounted for.

[
92
]

The rather numerous Jewish holy days,
together with the Muslim holy days, far exceed the two or three days available
for new holidays. Further, I suspect neither parents, teachers, society
generally, nor the school budget would tolerate lengthening the school year.

[
93
]

While once again contrary to the
Charter
,
another way suggested by the applicants would be to hold professional activity
days on religious holy days, thus relieving students from attending on those
days. Regulation 304 reads in part:

1(1) In this Regulation

"instructional day" means a school day that is
designated as an instructional day on a school calendar and upon which day an
instructional program that may include examinations is provided for each pupil
whose program is governed by such calendar;

"professional activity" includes evaluation of the
progress of pupils, consultation with parents, the counselling of pupils,
curriculum and program evaluation and development, professional development of
teachers and attendance at educational conferences;

"professional activity day" means a school day that
is designated as a day for professional activities on a school calendar;

* * * * *

2(2) Subject to section 5, a school year shall include a
minimum of 194 school days of which up to 9 days may be designated by the board
as professional activity days and the remaining school days shall be
instructional days.

[
94
]

The proposal to hold professional
activity days on holy days is only workable if professional activity days are
throw-away days that can be held at any time that will accommodate a holy day.
There is no evidence that professional activity days are so adaptable. If they
are, one has to wonder why they exist at all. If professional activity days are
less vital than instructional days, if they contribute less to learning by the
students than an instructional day, then they should be abolished.

[
95
]

Indeed, the only evidence on the point
is to the effect that professional activity days are not teacher holidays, that
they fill a vital purpose and so are unavailable to be shifted about to meet
the convenience of holy days.

[
96
]

While the applicants have watered down
the original request and now ask that the Board close two of its schools only —
Laurentian and Brookfield — both of which have a substantial number of Muslim
students, the same difficulties exist in attempting to close two schools as in
closing all of them.

[
97
]

Further, this application cannot be
considered on the basis of the provision of holidays for two Muslim holy days.
If Muslims are entitled to holidays for their holy days, so are Jews, Hindus and
all other religions. It is quite impossible to provide for all of them.

[
98
]

In short, no feasible way has been
suggested that would allow the schools to be closed to the students so as to
relieve Muslims and others from having to miss school on their holy days. Only
a wholesale revamping of the school year would accomplish the natural extension
of what is sought — school holidays on all holy days of all students. Such a
school year for the reasons I have given is not workable in today's society.

[
99
]

While in
CSR de Chambly
three
Jewish teachers were held entitled by way of accommodation to be paid for the
day they missed from work to observe Yom Kippur, that is a far cry from
demanding that all or some of the schools of the Board be
closed
to
students on two holy days.

[
100
]

Indeed, as I have already indicated,
the closing of schools for the celebration of religious holy days would in my
view be contrary to the
Charter
.
Atheists, agnostics and those not
affiliated with any religious denomination would have a legitimate complaint
that their right to a sensible school calendar was being sacrificed in the
interest of religion.

[
101
]

I am satisfied the Ottawa Board and the
Ministry have already taken reasonable steps to accommodate the Muslims and
others in regard to their holy days, including the following:

1. Students at schools of The Ottawa Board of Education,
including Brookfield and Laurentian, are allowed to be absent from school on
Muslim holy days for religious observance. This is the policy of the Board and
has been for several years in accordance with
s. 21(2)
(
g
) of the
Education
Act.

2. Since 1985 directives have been sent by the Board to all
schools with respect to the observance of holy days. On April 18, 1994, the
Board issued a directive with respect to the observance by students of holy
days, including Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha. This directive notes that teachers
should not schedule tests, exams or major co-curricular events on such holy
days. This is in accordance with Ministry of Education policy. The directive was
received by teachers at Laurentian and Brookfield.

3. The Board has taken a number of other steps in relation to
the observance of holy days by students. These include:

a) A multi-faith calendar describing the holy days of various
religions has been circulated throughout the schools of the Ottawa Board of
Education system.

b) A letter dated February 8, 1994 from Imam Ahmad Kutty of
the Islamic Foundation of Toronto with respect to the observance by students of
Ramadan and the festival of Eid-al-Fitr was circulated to all Board schools,
including Laurentian and Brookfield.

c) In 1979, the Board established a Multiculturalism Advisory
Committee to provide advice to the Board on matters of concern to the
ethno-cultural communities in the Ottawa area. This Committee acts as a two-way
link between the Board and ethnocultural communities, including the Muslim
community. Qasem Mahmud, the President of the Applicant Federation, has served
on this Committee and was its Chairman for several years.

d) The Board operates language classes in various schools
including the Arabic Iraqi School, the Somali Heritage Language School and the
Arabic Egyptian School. Representatives of these schools also serve on the
Multiculturalism Advisory Committee.

e) In 1984, the Board developed a written policy on racism and
ethnic relations. On the community consulting team which is now reviewing this
policy are two members of the Muslim community.

f) Starting in 1990, the Board established a policy that
meetings of the Board and its committees would not take place on religious holy
days.

4. Schools under the jurisdiction of the Board facilitate the
holding of noon prayers for Muslim students at school where required. In the
case of Laurentian, a prayer room was designated during the 1992-93 and the
1994-95 school years. (In 1993-94 no students made a request for a prayer
room.) At Brookfield, a prayer room has been designated for noon prayers for
the last three years. In addition, Muslim students at Brookfield have been able
to make announcements over the public address system in English and Arabic with
respect to Islamic faith observances and have used the auditorium for
presentations by Muslim spokespersons about the Islamic faith.

5. In addition, schools, and individual teachers accommodate
children absent for religious holidays (and for other legitimate reasons) by
providing small group or individualized tutoring. Accommodation must be
provided regardless of the number of students absent from the school on a
particular religious holiday. In fact, accommodation is often more difficult
when there are very few students away. If any teacher fails to follow
instructions and holds tests or exams on holy days and does not allow a student
to take a test or exam to make up for it, or does not otherwise assist the
student to make up what he has missed, then that teacher may be subject to
discipline. But the teacher's failure to follow instructions would not mean, at
least initially, that the Board had not accommodated its students.

6. In considering this accommodation issue, it is important to
keep in mind that, even apart from religious holidays, on any given day a
number of students are absent from school for a variety of legitimate reasons,
including sickness, field trips, and personal family matters. Further, it is
the rare student who does not miss at least some days during the regular school
year. Schools are already set up to accommodate such occasional, temporary
absences, and teachers expected to assist students and ensure that students are
not disadvantaged by such legitimate absences. Schools do not run on the
assumption that they will achieve 100% attendance on any given day, and they
are able to accommodate students who are absent for religious holidays in the
same way they can accommodate students who are absent for other legitimate
reasons.

[
102
]

In my view, the Board, the Ministry and
the Legislature itself have done what can reasonably be done to accommodate the
harm caused by adverse effect discrimination.

[
103
]

The Board's reasons for not declaring
school holidays or adjusting professional activity days for all or some of its
schools to accommodate the holy days of particular students or teachers in its
school may be summarized as follows:

The Board attempts to maintain a calendar that is consistent
with other Ottawa area boards in order to facilitate the transfer of students
and coordinate holidays for the convenience of families.

Board policy is to start the school year after the Labour Day
weekend and end it at the end of June.

It is desirable from an administrative and educational point
of view for teaching to be carried out, so far as possible, without
interruption for school holidays in the middle of a school week.

For the past 15 years the school calendar has included nine
professional activity days. In the secondary schools, six of these fall at the
end of the school year to allow for marking examinations, consultation with
parents and end-of-year preparations. Nine such days are required by the
collective agreements with teachers.

[
104
]

Even if professional activity days were
expendable (which they are not), there are not enough of them to cover the 13
Jewish religious holidays, the two Muslim holy days and the numerous other holy
days of particular religions, including the holy days of Orthodox and Eastern
Rite Christians which do not fall on the school holidays provided for by
Regulation 304.

[
105
]

The applicants made much of the fact
that the Board in 1994 delayed the first day of classes by two days on account
of the two Jewish holy days of Rosh Hashanah. As indicated, I accept this was
done to avoid problems that would otherwise exist for both teachers and Jewish
students if the Jewish students were to miss the orientation that occurs on
those days. Such did not become a precedent that Jews or anyone else could rely
on. The two holy days just happened to fall in 1994 on what would have been the
first two days of classes. That will not happen again for 30 or 40 years.
Further, the request for delay in commencement of classes was supported by the
Multicultural Advisory Committee to which committee Muslim groups belong.
Because the Board accommodated the Jewish holy days for the reason stated on
such a rare occasion does not mean it must now find a way to accommodate every
holy day of every student by closing the schools on such holy days.

[
106
]

The applicants claim the Board brushed
aside their request for holidays on their holy days and did not consider it. It
appears to me that the Board entertained in its usual fashion the presentations
made to it on April 25, 1994 by Mr. Mahmud and Mr. Bhatti. Each was given the
usual 5 minutes allotted by the Board for such presentations. The fact no
member of the Board commented or asked questions does not mean the presentation
was being tolerated only.

[
107
]

Neither do I accept that the request by
the Muslims was not considered. It was considered and rejected. By letters of
May 3, 1994 and May 16, 1994, Brian McGarry, Chairperson of The Ottawa Board of
Education, made it quite clear to counsel for the applicants that the Board did
not intend to recognize religious holy days as school holidays.

Conclusion

[
108
]

Regulation 304 creates secular, not
religious, school holidays. The purpose of the Regulation is neutral in regard
to religion and so does not offend the
Charter
's guarantees of freedom
of conscience and religion, and equal protection and benefit of the law without
discrimination. Since s. 21(2)(
g
) of the
Education Act
excuses a
child from school on his holy days, Regulation 304 does not have the adverse
effect of infringing the Muslims' freedom of conscience and religion guaranteed
by
s. 2
(a)
of the
Charter.

[
109
]

As to whether the Muslims have been
caused adverse effect discrimination by the impugned paragraphs of Regulation
304 on the basis that Christians celebrate their holy days of Good Friday,
Easter Monday and Christmas Day during school holidays while the Muslims must
miss school on theirs, I note that Easter Monday is not a holy day and that
Good Friday at least in the Roman Catholic Church is not a holy day of
obligation. There is no evidence that any appreciable number of Christian
students of the Ottawa Board attend church services on, or otherwise observe or
celebrate, the religious significance of Christmas Day, Good Friday or Easter
Monday. There is then no foundation in the evidence for the proposition that
Christian students celebrate their holy days on school holidays while Muslims
have to miss school to celebrate theirs.

[
110
]

If one assumes without evidence that
such adverse effect discrimination exists, then Regulation 304 remains valid
because the legislature, in pursuing the necessary goal of providing for school
holidays, has chosen secular holidays that coincide with those enjoyed by the
majority of the community and could not have chosen holidays that interfere
less with the Muslims' right to equal protection and benefit of the law.
Further, if there be any infringement of that right, such is demonstrably
justified as being a reasonable limit on that right in a free and democratic
society. Regulation 304 does not then offend the
Charter
.

[
111
]

Assuming again that Muslim students
suffer adverse effect discrimination by having to miss school on their holy
days then the Ottawa Board and the Ministry have provided reasonable
accommodation, short of hardship to the Muslims, in many ways, but in
particular by directing the school teachers to assist the students to catch up
on any lessons missed.

[
112
]

Further, the Ottawa Board did not
ignore the request of the applicants that it declare holidays for the Muslim
holy days of Eid-al-Fitr and Eid-al-Adha. Rather, the Board rejected that
request and the request that it study the issue of holidays on religious holy
days, and the Board so informed the applicants.

[
113
]

The application is dismissed in its
entirety with costs to the Board fixed at $7,500.00.

[
114
]

Application dismissed.
